summary_en: Raised by Liang Ji after Emperor Chong's death, he was eight; his sharp tongue called Liang Ji the "arrogant general," and in the first Benchu year he was poisoned, Liang Ji enthroning Emperor Huan.

bio_md:
# 汉质帝 · 主要事迹

刘缵是渤海孝王刘鸿之子。永嘉元年[[e-han-chong|冲帝]]崩，梁太后与梁冀定策，迎年八岁的刘缵即位，是为质帝。这是他悲剧的开端，也是东汉梁氏专权最盛的时刻。

质帝幼而聪慧，史称「少聪敏」。本初元年，他在朝堂上直视梁冀，说了一句改变命运的话——「此跋扈将军也」。梁冀深恶之，同年闰六月，进毒饼弑帝。质帝中毒后尚能饮水求活，梁冀不许，帝遂崩，在位不过一年余。史家多惜其聪慧而哀其早夭：一个八岁的孩子，因为一句真话，成了东汉皇权与权臣对决的第一个牺牲品。

质帝死后，梁冀迎立蠡吾侯[[e-han-huan|刘志]]，是为桓帝。梁氏之祸又延续了十三年，直到延熹二年桓帝与宦官合谋诛梁氏。质帝之死是梁冀权势的注脚，也是东汉士人对「跋扈」一词最早的集体记忆——「跋扈将军」由此成为权臣的千古恶谥。

> 参考：点校本《后汉书》卷006《孝质帝纪》、《梁冀传》，谭图第 2 册。

bio_parts_en.value: Liu Zuan was the son of the filial king Hong of Bohai. In the first Yongjia year, after

died, Empress Dowager Liang and Liang Ji chose the eight-year-old Zuan as Emperor Zhi. That was the beginning of his tragedy, and the summit of Liang autocracy in Eastern Han.

Zhi was sharp-witted as a child; the histories say he was "quick and clever from youth." In the first Benchu year, looking straight at Liang Ji in the court, he said the words that changed his life — "This is the arrogant general." Liang Ji hated him for it, and in the intercalary sixth month of the same year had poisoned cakes brought to the emperor. The poisoned boy begged for water to save himself; Liang Ji refused, and the emperor died, having reigned a little over a year. Historians have pitied the sharp boy and mourned his early end: an eight-year-old, killed for one true sentence, the first victim of the duel between Han sovereignty and its overbearing minister.

After Zhi's death Liang Ji raised the marquis of Liwu,

, as Emperor Huan, and the Liang scourge ran another thirteen years until Huan destroyed it with the eunuchs in the second Yanxi year. Zhi's death is the footnote to Liang Ji's power, and the origin of the士人's collective memory of the word "arrogant" — "the arrogant general" has been the eternal epithet of the overbearing minister ever since.

> References: the punctuated critical edition of the *Hou Hanshu*, ch. 6 (Benji of Emperor Zhi) and the biography of Liang Ji; Tan Qixiang's atlas, vol. 2.
